30.stem: A pulmonary contusion is BEST described as:
choices: Bruising of lung tissue that impairs gas exchange and may worsen over hours
Air trapped only in the subcutaneous space of the neck
A clean break of a single rib with no lung involvement
Fluid overload from left-sided heart failure alone
30.why: Contused lung bleeds/leaks into alveoli → hypoxia that can sneak up after the crash.

30.stem: After blunt chest trauma, progressive hypoxia with crackles and present bilateral breath sounds MOST suggests:
choices: Pulmonary contusion
Simple tension physiology with tracheal shift as the first finding
Uncomplicated anxiety hyperventilation
Isolated soft-tissue contusion of the chest wall
30.why: Contusion: lungs still make sound, but oxygenation slides downhill as tissue stiffens.

30.stem: Traumatic asphyxia occurs when:
choices: Sudden severe chest compression forces blood into the head and neck
A patient hyperventilates from panic alone
Only a single finger is crushed
A mild cough raises venous pressure briefly
30.why: Crush → retrograde venous flow → purple face/neck, petechiae, conjunctival hemorrhage.

30.stem: Classic signs of traumatic asphyxia include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Cyanotic, swollen face and neck
Petechiae of the face or conjunctiva
Sharp color change often above the clavicles
Isolated ankle swelling with warm dry skin
30.why: Head/neck congestion is the hallmark. Distal extremity edema is not the pattern.

30.stem: Myocardial contusion should be suspected after blunt chest trauma when the patient has:
choices: Chest pain, irregular pulse, or signs resembling cardiac ischemia
Only a sprained wrist
Clear lungs and zero chest discomfort forever
Fever and productive cough starting days later only
30.why: Bruised myocardium behaves like ACS — dysrhythmias and pump trouble are the worry.

30.stem: EMT care for suspected myocardial contusion emphasizes:
choices: High-flow oxygen as needed, monitor for dysrhythmias/shock, rapid transport
Home observation with NSAIDs only
Needle decompression as a first-line EMT skill
Forceful chest percussion to 'clear' the bruise
30.why: Support ABCs and move them — hospital rules out contusion vs ischemia vs tamponade.

30.stem: Best field care for isolated rib fractures includes:
choices: Oxygen if needed, position of comfort, encourage careful deep breaths, transport
Tight circumferential taping of the entire chest
Withholding all pain relief so they breathe shallow forever
Immediate needle decompression bilaterally
30.why: Splinting too tightly → atelectasis/pneumonia. Coach breathing; don't strap the chest shut.

30.stem: Elderly patients with rib fractures are at increased risk for:
choices: Pneumonia and respiratory failure from shallow breathing
Immediate full recovery without complications
Only cosmetic bruising with no pulmonary concern
Guaranteed tension pneumothorax in every case
30.why: Pain → shallow breaths → atelectasis. Geriatric ribs + lungs = higher stakes.

30.stem: Complications of rib fractures include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Pneumothorax
Hemothorax
Pulmonary contusion
Isolated uncomplicated toenail avulsion
30.why: Broken ribs threaten the lung and vessels underneath — not distant digits.

30.stem: A commercial vented chest seal or tape on three sides is preferred for an open chest wound because it:
choices: Limits air entry while allowing trapped air a path out
Completely prevents any possibility of tension forever
Replaces the need for oxygen or transport
Forces the lung to reinflate instantly on scene
30.why: One-way / vented concept reduces entrainment and gives a release path if pressure builds.

30.stem: Fully sealing an open pneumothorax on all four sides without a vent raises concern for:
choices: Conversion to tension pneumothorax if air cannot escape
Guaranteed resolution of all chest injuries
Immediate improvement of venous return only
Elimination of the need to reassess breathing
30.why: No vent + ongoing leak into pleural space = tension risk. Reassess constantly.

30.stem: After sealing a sucking chest wound, you must continuously monitor for:
choices: Worsening dyspnea, JVD, hypotension, and absent sounds on the injured side
Only improved appetite
Hypertension as the expected early finding
Bilateral wheezes as the sole concern
30.why: Your seal can create tension. Watch perfusion and the injured-side lung.

30.stem: If a sealed open chest wound patient deteriorates with signs of tension, the EMT should FIRST:
choices: Briefly lift (burp) a corner of the dressing to release trapped air
Perform needle decompression as a routine EMT skill
Tighten the seal completely on all four sides
Ignore the change and continue without reassessment
30.why: Burp the seal. Needle decompression is ALS — not your first EMT move.

30.stem: Needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax is:
choices: An ALS / paramedic-level intervention, not a standard EMT skill
Required for every EMT on every rib fracture
Preferred over oxygen for mild chest wall bruising
Used prophylactically before sealing any wound
30.why: EMT: seal, O2, burp if needed, rapid transport / ALS intercept. Leave the needle to ALS.

30.stem: Injury to the aorta or other great vessels after high-energy blunt trauma often presents with:
choices: Rapid deterioration into profound shock with little external bleeding
Always a painless, stable course for days
Only a minor finger laceration
Hypertension that never progresses
30.why: Great-vessel disruption = catastrophic internal hemorrhage. Load and go.

30.stem: Which MOI MOST raises suspicion for traumatic aortic injury?
choices: High-speed deceleration MVC or fall from significant height
Low-energy paper cut to a finger
Chronic stable angina without trauma
Mild sneeze with no chest impact
30.why: Sudden stop shears the aorta at ligamentum arteriosum. Think high energy.

30.stem: A diaphragmatic rupture from blunt trauma may allow:
choices: Abdominal contents to herniate into the chest, impairing ventilation
Only cosmetic changes with perfect breathing
Immediate resolution without imaging
Guaranteed bilateral equal breath sounds forever
30.why: Bowel in the thorax = bad lung expansion. Often left-sided; high MOI.

30.stem: Suspect diaphragmatic injury when chest trauma includes:
choices: Bowel sounds in the chest or marked respiratory distress after abdominal impact
Isolated epistaxis with clear lungs and no MOI
A sprained ankle only
Normal exam after a trivial bump
30.why: Herniated gut can sound (and act) like a chest problem. High suspicion after crush/MVC.

30.stem: An open chest injury differs from a closed chest injury primarily because:
choices: The chest wall/skin is penetrated, allowing communication with the outside air
Closed injuries never involve internal organs
Open injuries never cause shock
Only closed injuries need oxygen
30.why: Open = break in the wall/skin. Closed can still kill (contusion, tamponade, vessels).

30.stem: Paradoxical chest wall motion means the flail segment:
choices: Moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration
Moves exactly like the rest of the chest at all times
Only occurs with ankle fractures
Is always painless and cosmetic
30.why: Unstable segment gets sucked in when the patient inhales — opposite of normal.

30.stem: Preferred EMT support for a hypoxic flail-chest patient is:
choices: Assist ventilations with BVM and high-concentration oxygen as needed
Circumferential tape tight enough to stop all chest motion
Needle decompression of both sides before assessing ABCs
Oral fluids and delayed transport
30.why: PPV can internally splint. Don't strap the whole chest shut; don't delay.

30.stem: What BEST separates tension pneumothorax from a simple pneumothorax?
choices: Hemodynamic compromise (shock, JVD) from rising intrathoracic pressure
Mild unilateral pain with completely stable vitals forever
Fever and productive cough as the first signs
Equal bilateral clear sounds with normal perfusion
30.why: Simple = lung problem. Tension = lung + vena cava compression → shock.

30.stem: Compared with tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax more often shows:
choices: Flat neck veins and signs of blood-loss shock with dullness on one side
Bounding hypertension as the earliest finding
Always loud wheezes bilaterally
No effect on perfusion
30.why: Blood in the chest = hypovolemia → flat veins. Tension air = backed-up veins.

30.stem: Equal bilateral breath sounds with Beck-type findings after penetrating chest trauma favor:
choices: Cardiac tamponade over tension pneumothorax
Simple asthma exacerbation
Isolated soft-tissue bruise only
Guaranteed pulmonary contusion alone
30.why: Tamponade: heart squeezed, lungs often clear/equal. Tension: unilateral absent sounds.

30.stem: Crepitus under the skin of the chest or neck after trauma most often indicates:
choices: Air leaking into soft tissues from airway or lung injury
Normal finding in all healthy athletes
Only a skin infection requiring antibiotics on scene
Guaranteed benign outcome with no further evaluation
30.why: Sub-Q air = something is leaking. Look for pneumothorax / airway injury.

30.stem: After applying an occlusive dressing to an open chest wound, reassessment should occur:
choices: Frequently — watch for tension physiology and worsening distress
Never again until hospital arrival
Only if the patient requests it
Once, then ignore vitals
30.why: Dressings change physiology. Recheck breathing, sounds, and perfusion often.

30.stem: Priority management for a dyspneic patient with an open chest wound and a non-life-threatening extremity fracture is:
choices: Seal the chest and oxygenate first, then address other injuries en route
Splint the arm before touching the chest wound
Delay sealing until a full secondary survey is finished on scene
Give oral fluids before any wound care
30.why: Airway/breathing first. Seal and O2 beat orthopedic housekeeping.

30.stem: After steering-wheel impact, assume possible injury to all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Heart (contusion/tamponade risk)
Lungs (contusion/pneumothorax)
Great vessels
Isolated calcaneus fracture as the only possible injury
30.why: Chest MOI threatens heart, lungs, vessels — not 'only a heel.'

30.stem: Shallow, rapid breathing after chest trauma reduces minute ventilation mainly by:
choices: Cutting tidal volume so much that faster rate may not compensate
Always increasing alveolar ventilation to super-normal levels
Eliminating all dead-space gas automatically
Guaranteeing SpO2 of 100% without oxygen
30.why: Tiny breaths × fast rate still = poor alveolar ventilation. Support as needed.

30.stem: The pleural space normally:
choices: Is a potential space; air or blood there collapses lung tissue
Is filled with several liters of free air in healthy people
Contains the entire small intestine in normal anatomy
Cannot be entered by penetrating trauma
30.why: Air (pneumo) or blood (hemo) in the pleural space takes up room the lung needs.

30.stem: Tracheal deviation away from the injured side in tension pneumothorax is:
choices: A late finding — do not wait for it to treat deteriorating physiology
The earliest and most reliable first sign in every patient
Proof that the patient is stable
Required before applying oxygen
30.why: Shock + unilateral silence matter first. Tracheal shift is late and unreliable.

30.stem: A sucking chest wound impairs ventilation primarily because:
choices: Air prefers the wound path over the trachea, reducing effective lung inflation
It always seals itself within seconds
It only affects the opposite uninjured lung forever
It raises atmospheric oxygen concentration
30.why: Hole = path of least resistance. Seal it so air goes down the airway again.

30.stem: An impaled object in the chest should be:
choices: Stabilized in place with bulky dressings unless it blocks the airway or CPR
Removed immediately by the EMT in all cases
Pushed deeper to 'seat' it
Ignored while you focus only on distal pulses
30.why: Object may tamponade bleeding. Stabilize; OR removes it (rare airway exceptions).

30.stem: High-concentration oxygen is indicated for chest-trauma patients who are:
choices: Hypoxic, dyspneic, or showing signs of respiratory compromise / shock
Asymptomatic with SpO2 99% and no distress after a paper cut
Never allowed oxygen after any trauma
Only given oxygen after needle decompression by EMTs
30.why: Support oxygenation early. Don't withhold for 'waiting on ALS procedures.'

30.stem: Unstable chest-trauma patients generally need:
choices: Rapid transport to an appropriate trauma facility with ongoing ABCs
Prolonged scene time for every nonessential bandage
Oral challenge of fluids before leaving
Discharge home if pain improves slightly
30.why: Chest trauma that makes them sick is a surgical clock. Package and go.

30.stem: For a conscious patient with suspected simple pneumothorax, EMT priorities include:
choices: Oxygen, supportive positioning, monitor for tension, rapid transport
Immediate bilateral needle decompression by the EMT
Encouraging forced breath-holding contests
Tight chest binders that eliminate all expansion
30.why: Support and watch for conversion. Needles are ALS when tension develops.

30.stem: Jugular venous distention in chest trauma may indicate all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Obstruction of venous return
Guaranteed mild anxiety with no thoracic injury
30.why: JVD + trauma = think tension or tamponade until proven otherwise.

30.stem: A narrowing pulse pressure after penetrating chest trauma should raise concern for:
choices: Pericardial tamponade limiting ventricular filling
Always a simple ankle sprain
Only dehydration from missing lunch
Hyperthyroidism as the primary field diagnosis
30.why: Filling is blocked → diastolic rises toward systolic. Classic tamponade clue.

30.stem: In children, significant internal chest injury can occur:
choices: With little external chest-wall deformity because the chest is more compliant
Only after obvious flail segments are visible
Never from blunt force
Only if three ribs are fractured in two places every time
30.why: Pliable pediatric chests hide force — contusion/visceral injury without many fractures.

30.stem: Acceptable materials for an occlusive chest seal include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Commercial vented chest seal
Petroleum gauze or plastic taped appropriately per protocol
Glove or foil used as an improvised occlusive layer when needed
Dry fluffy gauze alone left completely open to free airflow
30.why: You need an airtight (or vented one-way) barrier — plain open gauze still sucks.

31.stem: A seat-belt sign across the abdomen after an MVC means:
choices: Possible intra-abdominal or lumbar injury even if vitals are still normal
Guaranteed absence of internal injury
Only a cosmetic bruise needing ice at home
That the belt failed and no force was transmitted
31.why: Belt mark = energy went into the belly. Compensated patients still need trauma eval.

31.stem: Kehr sign is:
choices: Left shoulder pain referred from diaphragmatic irritation, often splenic injury
Right calf pain from a simple sprain
Ear pain from otitis media
Numbness of the little toe only
31.why: Blood under the left diaphragm → left shoulder. Think spleen.

31.stem: LUQ tenderness after left-rib trauma plus left shoulder pain MOST suggests:
choices: Splenic injury with referred diaphragmatic pain
Isolated right-ankle fracture
Uncomplicated GERD without trauma relevance
Guaranteed appendicitis only
31.why: LUQ + Kehr = spleen until proven otherwise.

31.stem: Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) conceptually suggests:
choices: Retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal bleeding tracking to the umbilicus
A harmless skin rash unrelated to trauma
Only a superficial bee sting
Guaranteed normal CT findings
31.why: Late bruising around the umbilicus flags deep bleeding — high index of suspicion.

31.stem: Grey Turner sign (flank bruising) conceptually indicates:
choices: Possible retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Isolated contact dermatitis from clothing dye
Always a pulmonary embolism
Normal finding after light jogging
31.why: Flank ecchymosis = think retroperitoneal blood (kidney/pancreas/etc.).

31.stem: The KEY clinical difference is that hollow-organ rupture tends to cause ___ while solid-organ injury tends to cause ___.
choices: Peritonitis from spillage; hemorrhage from vascular parenchyma
Immediate massive bleeding only; never infection
Identical field presentations with no distinction
Only cosmetic pain; never shock
31.why: Hollow spills → chemical/bacterial peritonitis. Solid bleeds → shock.

31.stem: Hollow-organ injury may initially look subtle because:
choices: Peritonitis from spilled contents can develop over time
Hollow organs never injure
Spill always causes instant hypertension
Patients always remain asymptomatic forever
31.why: Chemical peritonitis builds. Early exams can underestimate hollow injury.

31.stem: Solid-organ hemorrhage is dangerous in the field mainly because:
choices: Large blood loss can hide inside the abdomen until shock appears
It never causes tachycardia
It only causes delayed itching
External bleeding always reveals the full volume lost
31.why: Abdomen holds liters. MOI + soft signs → treat for shock early.

31.stem: Unstable pelvic fracture with GU findings should prompt the EMT to:
choices: Bind/stabilize the pelvis, limit movement, treat shock, rapid transport
Rock the pelvis repeatedly to 'confirm' instability
Insert a Foley catheter on scene despite blood at the meatus
Encourage ambulation to reduce pain
31.why: Pelvis bleeds big. Bind, don't rock, don't catheterize through a torn urethra.

31.stem: Blood at the urethral meatus after pelvic trauma means:
choices: Possible urethral injury — do not insert a urinary catheter in the field
That catheterization is required immediately by EMTs
A trivial finding with no further concern
Guaranteed bladder infection only
31.why: Meatal blood = urethral tear risk. No blind Foley. Let the hospital image/repair.

31.stem: Which finding is a contraindication to field urinary catheterization after trauma?
choices: Blood at the meatus, perineal hematoma, or high-riding prostate (hospital finding)
Mild thirst alone
A healed old scar on the elbow
Stable vitals after a finger laceration
31.why: Signs of urethral disruption = don't push a catheter through the injury.

31.stem: External genital laceration bleeding is BEST controlled by:
choices: Direct pressure with sterile dressings; preserve privacy and dignity
Packing the vaginal canal as a routine EMT skill
Application of a pelvic tourniquet
Ignoring hemorrhage to protect 'modesty' at all costs
31.why: External pressure works. Don't pack internally. Treat bleeding and be respectful.

31.stem: Significant scrotal trauma with swelling and pain warrants:
choices: Supportive care, ice if protocol allows, and transport for evaluation
On-scene surgical exploration by EMTs
Forceful reduction of any swelling manually
Discharge without exam if the patient can walk
31.why: Testicular injury and urethral injury need hospital eval — support and go.

31.stem: A third-trimester trauma patient on a backboard should generally be:
choices: Tilted left lateral (or uterus displaced left) to reduce vena cava compression
Kept strictly flat supine for the entire transport without tilt
Placed prone to protect the airway only
Sat fully upright with no spinal considerations ever
31.why: Gravid uterus on the IVC → supine hypotension. Left tilt preserves venous return.

31.stem: In pregnant trauma, the BEST way to help the fetus is to:
choices: Resuscitate and oxygenate the mother aggressively; treat her shock
Ignore maternal ABCs and focus only on fetal heart tones on scene
Withhold oxygen to avoid 'too much' for the mother
Delay transport for a prolonged secondary survey
31.why: Mom's perfusion = baby's perfusion. Fix mother first; move to trauma OB care.

31.stem: An impaled object in the abdomen should be:
choices: Stabilized with bulky dressings and left in place for surgical removal
Removed immediately to inspect the tract
Advanced deeper before transport
Twisted to assess depth
31.why: Tamponade effect. Stabilize, control bleeding around it, OR pulls it.

31.stem: Shortening an impaled object is ONLY considered when:
choices: It prevents packaging or transport and can be done without rocking the wound
The EMT wants a souvenir
Pain is mild
Vitals are normal so removal is 'safe'
31.why: Leave length unless logistics force a careful cut — never yank it out.

31.stem: Rebound tenderness suggests:
choices: Peritoneal irritation — press gently, release, pain worsens on release
That the abdomen is completely normal
Only muscular strain with no intra-abdominal concern
A need for repeated deep poking to map every organ
31.why: Pain on release = peritonitis clue. Don't torture the belly with endless deep exams.

31.stem: Voluntary or involuntary abdominal guarding after trauma indicates:
choices: Possible peritonitis or significant intra-abdominal injury
Reliable proof of no injury
That oral antacids are first-line field care
A primary psychiatric diagnosis
31.why: Guarding = the peritoneum is unhappy. Treat for serious injury.

31.stem: Referred abdominal pain patterns include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Liver injury → right shoulder
Spleen injury → left shoulder (Kehr)
Diaphragmatic irritation → shoulder pain
Appendicitis → pain exclusively in the left little finger
31.why: Shoulder referral from diaphragm is classic. Finger tip pain is not the pattern.

31.stem: Organs primarily in the LUQ include:
choices: Spleen and much of the stomach
Appendix and ascending colon only
Gallbladder alone
Prostate only
31.why: LUQ: spleen, stomach. Appendix is RLQ; gallbladder RUQ.

31.stem: RLQ pain after trauma or illness most often raises concern for involvement of the:
choices: Appendix / cecum region (and nearby structures)
Spleen exclusively
Left kidney only
Entire right lung apex only
31.why: RLQ = appendix territory. Trauma can also hit cecum/ileum — know your map.

31.stem: Kidneys are considered retroperitoneal, which means bleeding may:
choices: Hide without early peritoneal signs while still causing significant blood loss
Always produce immediate rigid abdomen
Never cause hematuria
Only appear as a cough
31.why: Retroperitoneal space masks volume. Flank MOI + hematuria = serious.

31.stem: Blunt flank trauma with bruising and urinary complaints should make you think:
choices: Kidney injury until proven otherwise
Isolated soft-tissue bruise with zero GU risk
Always a tension pneumothorax first
Need for immediate Foley by EMTs every time
31.why: Flank = kidney zone. Support, monitor shock, transport — no blind catheters.

31.stem: Besides moist sterile coverage, eviscerated organs should be:
choices: Kept warm (occlusive outer layer) and not replaced into the abdomen
Dried thoroughly with a heat gun
Pushed firmly back into the cavity on scene
Left uncovered for 'air drying'
31.why: Moist + warm + don't replace. Shock care and rapid transport.

31.stem: During the abdominal exam in trauma, you should:
choices: Inspect and gently palpate once; avoid repeated deep probing
Deeply palpate every quadrant repeatedly to 'confirm' bleeding
Skip the abdomen if the chest looks interesting
Percuss forcefully until the patient vomits
31.why: One careful exam. Repeated digging worsens bleeding and pain.

31.stem: Patients with suspected abdominal trauma should generally be:
choices: Kept NPO (nothing by mouth)
Encouraged to drink large volumes of water
Given solid snacks for comfort
Allowed alcohol to 'calm nerves'
31.why: Surgery risk + vomiting/aspiration. Nothing by mouth.

31.stem: Suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage with falling BP and rising pulse needs:
choices: High-flow O2 as indicated, keep warm, supine (tilt if late pregnant), rapid transport
Prolonged scene IV attempts before any packaging
Walking the patient to the ambulance to 'improve circulation'
Hot packs on the abdomen and delayed departure
31.why: Hemorrhagic shock = oxygen, warmth, position, and a short scene clock.

31.stem: Seat-belt or deceleration forces can tear the mesentery, which primarily causes:
choices: Bleeding and possible bowel ischemia from disrupted blood supply
Only a sore neck forever
Immediate resolution without risk
Guaranteed appendicitis in the LUQ
31.why: Mesentery holds gut vessels. Tear → bleed and threatened bowel.

31.stem: A stab wound to the upper abdomen can injure:
choices: Abdominal organs and, depending on angle/depth, thoracic structures
Only skin with no deeper concern if the hole looks small
Never the diaphragm
Only the contralateral foot
31.why: Trajectory matters. Small holes can hide big paths — chest and belly both.

31.stem: Closed abdominal injury means:
choices: Skin intact, usually blunt force — internal organs can still be devastated
No possibility of internal bleeding
Only open eviscerations count as serious
That transport can always wait overnight
31.why: Intact skin ≠ intact organs. Blunt belly kills quietly.

31.stem: Open abdominal injury implies:
choices: Penetration of the abdominal wall; assume organ involvement until proven otherwise
Automatic absence of infection risk
That evisceration never occurs
Only cosmetic repair is needed on scene
31.why: Penetrating wall = surgical evaluation. Dress, don't explore.

31.stem: Bladder injury is MORE likely when the bladder is:
choices: Full, especially with pelvic fracture or lower abdominal impact
Completely empty with no pelvic force
Protected solely by a soft seat cushion forever
Impossible to injure in MVCs
31.why: Full bladder + force or pelvic break = rupture risk. Watch for blood/urine issues.

31.stem: In pelvic trauma, inspecting the perineum (with privacy) is important because:
choices: Blood, bruising, or bleeding can signal urethral or pelvic injury
It replaces the need for vital signs
It is optional and never useful
It confirms that Foley placement is always safe
31.why: Perineal blood/hematoma flags GU injury — and argues against blind catheterization.

31.stem: Direct compression of the abdomen (e.g., against a steering wheel) commonly risks:
choices: Solid-organ rupture and hollow-organ crush/tear
Only a bruised ego
Guaranteed exclusive ankle injury
No visceral injury if skin is intact
31.why: Compression smooshes liver/spleen and can burst hollow organs.

31.stem: Deceleration abdominal injuries often involve:
choices: Shearing of organs or vessels at attachment points (e.g., liver, mesentery)
Only injuries to fingernail beds
Injuries that appear only after two weeks every time
Zero risk if the patient was restrained
31.why: Organs keep moving when the body stops — attachments tear. Belts help but don't erase risk.

31.stem: A patient with peritonitis often prefers which position?
choices: Still, often with knees flexed to reduce abdominal wall tension
Forceful sit-ups to 'work out' the pain
Prone press-ups repeatedly
Jogging in place
31.why: Knees up, lying still — movement hurts inflamed peritoneum.

31.stem: Pediatric abdominal trauma is concerning because children:
choices: Have less protection and can compensate until sudden decompensation
Never bleed significantly from solid organs
Always show early hypotension
Do not need trauma centers after high MOI
31.why: Kids look okay, then crash. MOI drives destination more than a single BP.

31.stem: An open abdominal wound without evisceration should be:
choices: Covered with a sterile dressing (moist if protocol/exposed tissue) and monitored for shock
Packed with ice directly into the cavity
Left open to collect debris
Explored with fingers to count organs
31.why: Clean cover, shock care, transport. No digital exploration.

31.stem: Which statement BEST reflects EMT priorities for serious abdominal trauma?
choices: Limited scene time, ABCs, hemorrhage control, rapid transport to surgery-capable care
Complete every nonessential bandaging before leaving
Wait on scene until rebound tenderness appears
Needle decompress the abdomen as an EMT skill
31.why: Bleeders need surgeons. Seal/cover, O2, warmth, and go — no abdominal needles.
